Chapter 1: Searching for Purpose and Facing the Unknown
Have you ever felt that nagging restlessness, like your life’s routines are just going through the motions? Maybe it’s a quiet ache—a sense that something important is missing, but you can’t quite put your finger on it.
Picture a teenager in the suburbs of mid-century America, feeling exactly that. He’s caught in a tug-of-war between what his family expects and this growing pull for something deeper. Everything around him—school, church, maybe even a future in medicine—feels mapped out already. But none of it answers those questions that keep him up at night.
What if faith was more than just rituals and rules? What if real meaning was waiting somewhere far beyond what’s familiar?
As the years passed, that longing for something genuine only grew stronger. At home, conversations about religion often turned into heated debates. His dad, especially, saw faith as a set of boundaries—a way to keep life safe and predictable. But our young friend just couldn’t shake the feeling that faith was supposed to be risky, maybe even a little wild.
He read about people who gave up everything to follow what they believed in, and wondered, could he ever do something that bold?
School didn’t offer much comfort, either. The lessons felt disconnected from the questions that really mattered to him. Even church, with its polished sermons and practiced hymns, seemed to dodge the rawness of real belief. The more he searched for answers, the more alone he felt. Friends couldn’t understand why he was so restless. Teachers brushed off his questions. At home, his parents started worrying he was drifting away from the path they’d hoped he’d follow.
Then one day, wandering through the library, he stumbled on a book about indigenous tribes deep in South America. These were people living in the jungle, untouched by modern life, who’d never even heard the name of Jesus. The idea of bringing faith to someone who’d never encountered it—well, it was both terrifying and thrilling. His heart raced at the thought.
But dreams like that rarely fit neatly into what others have planned for us, do they? When he shared his hopes with his parents, they were horrified. The jungle? It was dangerous—disease, violence, isolation. Why throw away a promising future for a fantasy? Even church leaders, who talked about missions from the pulpit, hesitated when faced with someone actually willing to go.
They offered polite encouragement, but nothing more.
Still, that pull just wouldn’t let go. So, he started saving every dollar he could, working odd jobs and cutting expenses wherever possible. He wrote letters to mission organizations, hoping for support, but most never replied. The ones that did told him he was too young, too inexperienced, maybe even too reckless.
Doors kept closing, one after another, but the calling only grew stronger.
Eventually, he realized—if he waited for permission, he’d be waiting forever.
So, he made a decision: he’d step out on his own. It was both liberating and terrifying. He bought a one-way ticket to Venezuela, packed a small bag, and said goodbye to everything he’d ever known. No guarantees. No safety nets. Just this belief that faith, if it meant anything, had to be lived out where comfort and certainty ended.
The journey started with a mix of excitement and fear. The airport was a blur of faces and noise. As the plane lifted off, he looked out the window and wondered—would he ever see home again? The adventure he’d dreamed about for so long was finally real. The unknown stretched out before him like a vast, uncharted map.
Landing in Venezuela, the reality hit hard. The city was hot, chaotic, and completely unfamiliar. Communicating was a struggle—his high school Spanish only got him so far. Money was tight. Some nights, he slept in cheap hotels, or even on the floor of a church. Hunger and loneliness became his constant companions.
Yet, even in the middle of all that, there were moments of grace. A local pastor took him in for a few days, sharing food and encouragement. A missionary family invited him for dinner, telling stories of their own challenges and victories. These small acts of kindness reminded him—he wasn’t completely alone, even here.
As he learned more about the indigenous tribes, he realized reaching them would be harder than he ever imagined. The Motilone people, especially, were known for their isolation and hostility to outsiders. Stories circulated about missionaries who’d tried to make contact—some were driven away, some never returned. The jungle itself was a wall of danger, filled with threats both seen and unseen.
But those risks didn’t scare him off. In fact, they made his resolve even stronger. Bringing hope to people who’d never heard it before? That was worth any sacrifice. He started learning the language—new words and phrases every single day. He found anyone with experience and soaked up their advice, their warnings. Most people told him to quit, to go home before it was too late. But he kept going, convinced that real purpose could only be found by stepping into the unknown.
Looking back, it’s easy to see how naïve he was. The challenges ahead would push him in ways he couldn’t even imagine. But in those early days, that mix of fear and hope was enough to keep him moving forward.
Sometimes, the only way to find out what faith really means is to risk everything for it.
